claim: A major cause of human deafness and vestibular dysfunction is permanent loss of the mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear.
source: A major cause of human deafness and vestibular dysfunction is permanent loss of the mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the causes of human deafness and vestibular dysfunction.

claim: In non-mammalian vertebrates such as zebrafish, regeneration of missing hair cells can occur throughout life.
source: In non-mammalian vertebrates such as zebrafish, regeneration of missing hair cells can occur throughout life.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by prior research on zebrafish hair cell regeneration.

claim: The study performs single-cell RNA sequencing of the zebrafish inner ear at embryonic through adult stages to catalog the diversity of hair cells and non-sensory supporting cells.
source: Here, we perform single-cell RNA sequencing of the zebrafish inner ear at embryonic through adult stages to catalog the diversity of hair cells and non-sensory supporting cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The study identifies a putative progenitor population for hair cells and supporting cells.
source: We identify a putative progenitor population for hair cells and supporting cells, as well as distinct hair and supporting cell types in the maculae versus cristae.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct hair and supporting cell types exist in the maculae versus cristae.
source: We identify a putative progenitor population for hair cells and supporting cells, as well as distinct hair and supporting cell types in the maculae versus cristae.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hair cell and supporting cell types differ from those described for the lateral line system.
source: The hair cell and supporting cell types differ from those described for the lateral line system, a distributed mechanosensory organ in zebrafish in which most studies of hair cell regeneration have been conducted.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of the inner ear and lateral line datasets.

claim: In the maculae, two subtypes of hair cells share gene expression with mammalian striolar or extrastriolar hair cells.
source: In the maculae, we identify two subtypes of hair cells that share gene expression with mammalian striolar or extrastriolar hair cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and comparison with mammalian data.

claim: Hair cell subtypes occupy distinct spatial domains within the three macular organs (utricle, saccule, and lagena).
source: In situ hybridization reveals that these hair cell subtypes occupy distinct spatial domains within the three macular organs, the utricle, saccule, and lagena, consistent with the reported distinct electrophysiological properties of hair cells within these domains.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The spatial organization of hair cell subtypes is consistent with the reported distinct electrophysiological properties of hair cells within these domains.
source: In situ hybridization reveals that these hair cell subtypes occupy distinct spatial domains within the three macular organs, the utricle, saccule, and lagena, consistent with the reported distinct electrophysiological properties of hair cells within these domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial patterns observed and prior knowledge of electrophysiological properties.

claim: Primitive specialization of spatially distinct striolar and extrastriolar hair cells likely arose in the last common ancestor of fish and mammals.
source: These findings suggest that primitive specialization of spatially distinct striolar and extrastriolar hair cells likely arose in the last common ancestor of fish and mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the homology observed between zebrafish and mammalian hair cell types.

claim: The similarities of inner ear cell type composition between fish and mammals validate zebrafish as a relevant model for understanding inner ear-specific hair cell function and regeneration.
source: The similarities of inner ear cell type composition between fish and mammals validate zebrafish as a relevant model for understanding inner ear-specific hair cell function and regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative analysis of cell types between species.

claim: Hair cells are notoriously susceptible to damage from multiple types of insults, including noise and ototoxic drug exposure.
source: Hair cells are notoriously susceptible to damage from multiple types of insults, including noise and ototoxic drug exposure.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of auditory research.

claim: Studies of hair cell physiology in mammals are limited by the location of the inner ear within the temporal bone.
source: Studies of hair cell physiology in mammals are limited by the location of the inner ear within the temporal bone, which precludes many targeted manipulations and in vivo imaging beyond the neonatal stage.
evidence: This is a known limitation in the field of mammalian auditory research.

claim: Non-mammalian vertebrates such as birds and fish can regenerate hair cells of the auditory and vestibular systems that are lost due to injury.
source: Non-mammalian vertebrates such as birds and fish can regenerate hair cells of the auditory and vestibular systems that are lost due to injury (Stone and Cotanche, 2007; Monroe et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mammals, cochlear hair cell death leads to permanent hearing loss.
source: This differs from mammals, where cochlear hair cell death leads to permanent hearing loss (Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Yamasoba and Kondo, 2006), and limited regeneration of vestibular hair cells results in minimal recovery of function (Golub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Limited regeneration of vestibular hair cells in mammals results in minimal recovery of function.
source: This differs from mammals, where cochlear hair cell death leads to permanent hearing loss (Corwin and Cotanche, 1988; Yamasoba and Kondo, 2006), and limited regeneration of vestibular hair cells results in minimal recovery of function (Golub et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The zebrafish lateral line system has been widely used to study mechanisms of hair cell physiology.
source: Due to its accessibility for manipulation and imaging, the zebrafish lateral line system has been widely used to study mechanisms of hair cell physiology (Pickett and Raible, 2019; Sheets et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The lateral line is an external sensory system that allows aquatic vertebrates to detect local movement of water.
source: The lateral line is an external sensory system that allows aquatic vertebrates to detect local movement of water.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the lateral line system.

claim: Sensory organs of the lateral line, called neuromasts, contain hair cells and supporting cells that share properties with those of the inner ear.
source: Sensory organs of the lateral line, called neuromasts, contain hair cells and supporting cells that share properties with those of the inner ear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the lateral line system.

claim: Cells in the zebrafish inner ear are likely more similar to their mammalian counterparts than lateral line cells.
source: However, relative to the lateral line, cells in the zebrafish inner ear are likely more similar to their mammalian counterparts, raising the potential for it to be a more comparable system in which to study hair cell function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical and functional considerations.

claim: Zebrafish and mammals share several inner ear sensory organs.
source: Zebrafish and mammals share several inner ear sensory organs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate inner ear anatomy.

claim: Three semicircular canals with sensory end organs called cristae sense angular rotation of the head.
source: Three semicircular canals with sensory end organs called cristae sense angular rotation of the head.
evidence: This is established knowledge about inner ear anatomy and function.

claim: The utricular and saccular macula each with an associated otolith crystal detect linear acceleration and gravity.
source: Two additional sensory end organs detect linear acceleration and gravity: the utricular and saccular macula each with an associated otolith crystal (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about inner ear anatomy and function, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Fish lack a specific auditory structure such as the mammalian cochlea.
source: Fish lack a specific auditory structure such as the mammalian cochlea and instead sense sound through the saccule, utricle, and a third otolith organ, the lagena.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fish auditory anatomy.

claim: Fish sense sound through the saccule, utricle, and a third otolith organ, the lagena.
source: Fish lack a specific auditory structure such as the mammalian cochlea and instead sense sound through the saccule, utricle, and a third otolith organ, the lagena.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fish auditory anatomy.

claim: There is substantial evidence for all three otolith end organs being used for sound detection with diverse specializations across fishes.
source: Although historically the utricle was thought to be for vestibular function and the saccule and lagena analogous to the cochlea for sound detection, there is now substantial evidence for all three otolith end organs being used for sound detection with diverse specializations across fishes (Popper and Fay, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish exhibit behavioral responses to sound frequencies between 100 and 1200 Hz.
source: Zebrafish exhibit behavioral responses to sound frequencies between 100 and 1200 Hz (Zeddies and Fay, 2005; Bhandiwad et al., 2013), and neural responses up to 4000 Hz (Poulsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish exhibit neural responses to sound up to 4000 Hz.
source: Zebrafish exhibit behavioral responses to sound frequencies between 100 and 1200 Hz (Zeddies and Fay, 2005; Bhandiwad et al., 2013), and neural responses up to 4000 Hz (Poulsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In larval zebrafish, both saccule and utricle hair cells respond to vibration stimuli.
source: In larval zebrafish, both saccule and utricle hair cells respond to vibration stimuli, with the utricle responding to relatively lower frequencies than the saccule, as well as additive effects when both are stimulated (Yao et al., 2016; Favre-Bulle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The utricle responds to relatively lower frequencies than the saccule.
source: In larval zebrafish, both saccule and utricle hair cells respond to vibration stimuli, with the utricle responding to relatively lower frequencies than the saccule, as well as additive effects when both are stimulated (Yao et al., 2016; Favre-Bulle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are additive effects when both saccule and utricle are stimulated.
source: In larval zebrafish, both saccule and utricle hair cells respond to vibration stimuli, with the utricle responding to relatively lower frequencies than the saccule, as well as additive effects when both are stimulated (Yao et al., 2016; Favre-Bulle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Within the mammalian utricle and saccule, there are both morphological and spatial differences between hair cells.
source: Within the mammalian utricle and saccule, there are both morphological and spatial differences between hair cells (Lysakowski and Goldberg, 2004; Eatock and Songer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hair cells are broadly classified by their morphology and innervation, with Type I hair cells having calyx synapses surrounding the hair cell body and Type II hair cells having bouton synapses.
source: Hair cells are broadly classified by their morphology and innervation, with Type I hair cells having calyx synapses surrounding the hair cell body and Type II hair cells having bouton synapses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian hair cell classification.

claim: Both Type I and Type II cells can be found within the central region of the macular organs known as the striola and in the surrounding extrastriolar zones.
source: Both Type I and Type II cells can be found within the central region of the macular organs known as the striola and in the surrounding extrastriolar zones.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian hair cell distribution.

claim: Hair cells across striolar and extrastriolar regions vary in morphology, electrophysiology, and synaptic structure.
source: Although the role of spatial segregation into striolar versus extrastriolar zones has not been fully elucidated, hair cells across these regions vary in morphology, electrophysiology, and synaptic structure (Desai et al., 2005; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The striola is characterized by hair cells with taller ciliary bundles.
source: The striola is characterized by hair cells with taller ciliary bundles and encompasses a line of polarity reversal where hair cells change their stereocilia orientation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about striolar hair cells, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The striola encompasses a line of polarity reversal where hair cells change their stereocilia orientation.
source: The striola is characterized by hair cells with taller ciliary bundles and encompasses a line of polarity reversal where hair cells change their stereocilia orientation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about striolar hair cells, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: Distinct Type I and Type II hair cells, and in particular the calyx synapses typical of Type I cells, have not been identified in the maculae of fishes.
source: Whereas distinct Type I and Type II hair cells, and in particular the calyx synapses typical of Type I cells, have not been identified in the maculae of fishes, afferent innervation with some calyx-like properties has been reported in goldfish cristae (Lanford and Popper, 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of certain features in fish, with a citation noting an exception.

claim: Afferent innervation with some calyx-like properties has been reported in goldfish cristae.
source: Whereas distinct Type I and Type II hair cells, and in particular the calyx synapses typical of Type I cells, have not been identified in the maculae of fishes, afferent innervation with some calyx-like properties has been reported in goldfish cristae (Lanford and Popper, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity in the maculae, including those of zebrafish, has been previously noted.
source: Spatial heterogeneity in the maculae, including those of zebrafish, has also been previously noted (Chang et al., 1992; Platt, 1993; Collin et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The homologies of cells at the cellular and molecular levels have remained unknown.
source: However, the homologies of cells at the cellular and molecular levels have remained unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing efforts have generated a wealth of transcriptomic data from hair cells in several model systems.
source: Recent single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing efforts have generated a wealth of transcriptomic data from hair cells in several model systems, facilitating more direct comparison of cell types and gene regulatory networks between species.
evidence: This is a statement about recent advances in the field.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic data have recently been published for the zebrafish inner ear.
source: Although single-cell transcriptomic data have recently been published for the zebrafish inner ear (Jimenez et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2022), the diversity of hair cell and supporting cell subtypes has not been thoroughly analyzed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The diversity of hair cell and supporting cell subtypes in the zebrafish inner ear has not been thoroughly analyzed.
source: Although single-cell transcriptomic data have recently been published for the zebrafish inner ear (Jimenez et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2022), the diversity of hair cell and supporting cell subtypes has not been thoroughly analyzed.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Hair and supporting cells from the zebrafish inner ear and lateral line are transcriptionally distinct.
source: We find that hair and supporting cells from the zebrafish inner ear and lateral line are transcriptionally distinct, and that hair and supporting cells differ between the cristae and maculae.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hair and supporting cells differ between the cristae and maculae.
source: We find that hair and supporting cells from the zebrafish inner ear and lateral line are transcriptionally distinct, and that hair and supporting cells differ between the cristae and maculae.
evidence: This is a finding from the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: All distinct cell types are present during larval development and are maintained into adulthood.
source: All of these distinct cell types are present during larval development and are maintained into adulthood.
evidence: This is a finding from the developmental time series analysis in the manuscript.

claim: Computational comparison of hair cell types reveals homology with striolar and extrastriolar hair cell types in mammals.
source: In situ hybridization reveals that these hair cell subtypes occupy distinct spatial domains within the utricle, saccule, and lagena, and computational comparison of hair cell types reveals homology with striolar and extrastriolar hair cell types in mammals.
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis comparing zebrafish and mouse hair cell types.

claim: A total of 16,517 inner ear and lateral line cells were isolated from the initial dataset.
source: Within an initial dataset of 1.25 million cells from 1233 embryos spanning 18 timepoints between 18 and 96 hr (see Saunders et al., 2022 for more detail), a total of 16,517 inner ear and lateral line cells were isolated, combined, and re-processed using Monocle 3 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This describes the data processing and is shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inner ear nonsensory cells were identified by expression of the transcription factor gene sox10 in combination with inner ear supporting cell genes.
source: Inner ear nonsensory cells were identified by expression of the transcription factor gene sox10 (Dutton et al., 2009) in combination with inner ear supporting cell genes (stm, otog, otogl, otomp, tecta, and oc90; Figure 2C; Söllner et al., 2003; Kalka et al., 2019; Petko et al., 2008; Stooke-Vaughan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify cell types, supported by citations and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lateral line nonsensory cells were identified by expression of known markers fat1b, tfap2a, tnfsf10l3, lef1, cxcr4b, fgfr1a, and hmx3a.
source: Lateral line nonsensory cells were identified by expression of known markers fat1b, tfap2a, tnfsf10l3, lef1, cxcr4b, fgfr1a, and hmx3a (Figure 2D; Steiner et al., 2014; Thomas and Raible, 2019; McGraw et al., 2011; Haas and Gilmour, 2006; Lee et al., 2016; Feng and Xu, 2010).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify cell types, supported by citations and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Hair cells were identified by expression of the pan-hair cell genes otofb, cdh23, pcdh15a, ush1c, myo7aa, slc17a8, and cacna1da.
source: We identified hair cells by expression of the pan-hair cell genes otofb, cdh23, pcdh15a, ush1c, myo7aa, slc17a8, and cacna1da (Figure 2E; Chatterjee et al., 2015; Söllner et al., 2004; Seiler et al., 2005; Phillips et al., 2011; Ernest et al., 2000; Obholzer et al., 2008; Sheets et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify cell types, supported by citations and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Inner ear and lateral line hair cells are marked distinctly by strc and s100t.
source: Although many of these markers are at low abundance, these populations are marked distinctly by strc and s100t (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both hair cells and nonsensory supporting cells from the inner ear and lateral line formed distinct clusters.
source: Both hair cells and nonsensory supporting cells from the inner ear and lateral line formed distinct clusters, with nonsensory cells from the two mechanosensory organs showing greater distinction than hair cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Nonsensory cells from the inner ear and lateral line show greater distinction than hair cells.
source: Both hair cells and nonsensory supporting cells from the inner ear and lateral line formed distinct clusters, with nonsensory cells from the two mechanosensory organs showing greater distinction than hair cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PAGA analysis revealed strong connectivity within inner ear supporting cell clusters and within lateral line supporting cell clusters but little connectivity between them.
source: PAGA analysis revealed strong connectivity within inner ear supporting cell clusters and within lateral line supporting cell clusters but little connectivity between them (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the PAGA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The inner ear nonsensory cluster includes structural cells forming the otic capsule, identified by expression of col2a1a and matn4.
source: The inner ear nonsensory cluster includes structural cells forming the otic capsule, identified by expression of the extracellular matrix protein-encoding genes collagen type 2 a1a (col2a1a) and matrilin 4 (matn4) (Xu et al., 2018), as well as sensory supporting cells expressing lfng (Figure 3D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis, supported by a citation and shown in figures.

claim: Inner ear and lateral line supporting cells remain as distinct clusters even when structural matn4+ cells are excluded from analysis.
source: Inner ear and lateral line supporting cells remain as distinct clusters even when structural matn4+ cells are excluded from analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The combined dataset comprises 3246 inner ear cells separated into 10 groups based on unsupervised clustering.
source: The combined dataset comprises 3246 inner ear cells separated into 10 groups based on unsupervised clustering, with differentially expressed genes for each cluster shown in Figure 3E and Supplementary file 4.
evidence: This describes the integrated dataset and clustering results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Six clusters of hair cells were identified based on shared expression of myo6b, strc, lhfpl5a, and gfi1aa.
source: We identified six clusters of hair cells based on shared expression of myo6b, strc, lhfpl5a, and gfi1aa (Yu et al., 2020), a nascent hair cell cluster based on expression of atoh1a (Millimaki et al., 2007) and the Notch ligand dla (Riley et al., 1999), and two clusters of supporting cells based on expression of lfng and stm (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the cell type identification based on marker gene expression, supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: A nascent hair cell cluster was identified based on expression of atoh1a and the Notch ligand dla.
source: We identified six clusters of hair cells based on shared expression of myo6b, strc, lhfpl5a, and gfi1aa (Yu et al., 2020), a nascent hair cell cluster based on expression of atoh1a (Millimaki et al., 2007) and the Notch ligand dla (Riley et al., 1999), and two clusters of supporting cells based on expression of lfng and stm (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the cell type identification based on marker gene expression, supported by citations and shown in figures.

claim: Two clusters of supporting cells were identified based on expression of lfng and stm.
source: We identified six clusters of hair cells based on shared expression of myo6b, strc, lhfpl5a, and gfi1aa (Yu et al., 2020), a nascent hair cell cluster based on expression of atoh1a (Millimaki et al., 2007) and the Notch ligand dla (Riley et al., 1999), and two clusters of supporting cells based on expression of lfng and stm (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the cell type identification based on marker gene expression shown in figures.

claim: A putative progenitor cluster (cluster 0), enriched for cells from embryonic stages, is characterized by expression of genes such as fgfr2, fat1a, igsf3, and pard3bb.
source: An additional putative progenitor cluster (cluster 0), enriched for cells from embryonic stages, is characterized by expression of genes such as fgfr2 (Rohs et al., 2013), fat1a (Down et al., 2005), igsf3, and pard3bb (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the putative progenitor cluster based on gene expression, supported by citations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pseudotime trajectory analysis revealed two major trajectories toward hair cell and supporting cell clusters for both maculae and cristae.
source: Analysis revealed two major trajectories toward hair cell and supporting cell clusters for both maculae and cristae (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with distinct patterns of gene expression along each trajectory (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Average gene expression of the putative progenitor (Cluster 0) markers follow two patterns: decreasing along both hair cell and supporting cell trajectories (fgfr2 and igsf3) and decreasing only along the hair cell trajectory (fat1a and pard3bb).
source: We find that average gene expression of the putative progenitor (Cluster 0) markers follow two patterns: decreasing along both hair cell and supporting cell trajectories (fgfr2 and igsf3) and decreasing only along the hair cell trajectory (fat1a and pard3bb) (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The hair cell trajectory progresses first through a stage marked by expression of dla and then atoh1a.
source: The hair cell trajectory progresses first through a stage marked by expression of dla and then atoh1a (Cluster 2, Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Concurrent with decreasing expression of nascent hair cell genes, there is increasing expression of mature hair cell genes gfi1aa and myo6b.
source: Concurrent with decreasing expression of nascent hair cell genes, we observe increasing expression of mature hair cell genes gfi1aa and myo6b (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Along the supporting cell trajectory there is upregulation of supporting cell-specific markers, including stm and lfng.
source: Along the supporting cell trajectory we observed upregulation of supporting cell-specific markers, including stm and lfng (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The bifurcating lineage trajectories from Cluster 0 to hair and supporting cell clusters are consistent with the identification of Cluster 0 as a population of bipotent progenitors regulated by Notch signaling during early development.
source: These bifurcating lineage trajectories from Cluster 0 (Figure 4A) to hair and supporting cell clusters are consistent with the identification of Cluster 0 as a population of bipotent progenitors regulated by Notch signaling during early development (Haddon et al., 1998; Riley et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pseudotime analysis and prior knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: dla is expressed in supporting cells adjacent to myo6:GFP hair cells in both cristae and maculae.
source: We find that dla is expressed in supporting cells adjacent to myo6:GFP hair cells in both cristae and maculae, consistent with peripheral addition of new cells at the margins of the sensory patches.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: dla expression is consistent with peripheral addition of new cells at the margins of the sensory patches.
source: We find that dla is expressed in supporting cells adjacent to myo6:GFP hair cells in both cristae and maculae, consistent with peripheral addition of new cells at the margins of the sensory patches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dla expression pattern observed.

claim: Supporting cells comprise two major clusters that can be distinguished by expression of tectb and zpld1a among other genes.
source: Supporting cells comprise two major clusters that can be distinguished by expression of tectb and zpld1a among other genes (Figure 3C, see Supplementary file 7 for differentially expressed genes).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering and differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The tectb gene encodes Tectorin beta, a component of the tectorial membrane associated with cochlear hair cells in mammals.
source: The tectb gene encodes Tectorin beta, a component of the tectorial membrane associated with cochlear hair cells in mammals (Goodyear et al., 2017), and a component of otoliths in zebrafish (Kalka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: tectb is a component of otoliths in zebrafish.
source: The tectb gene encodes Tectorin beta, a component of the tectorial membrane associated with cochlear hair cells in mammals (Goodyear et al., 2017), and a component of otoliths in zebrafish (Kalka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The zpld1a gene, encoding Zona-pellucida-like domain containing protein 1 a, is expressed in the cristae in fish.
source: The zpld1a gene, encoding Zona-pellucida-like domain containing protein 1 a, is expressed in the cristae in fish (Dernedde et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011) and mouse (Vijayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: zpld1a is expressed in the cristae in mouse.
source: The zpld1a gene, encoding Zona-pellucida-like domain containing protein 1 a, is expressed in the cristae in fish (Dernedde et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011) and mouse (Vijayakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: tectb is expressed in the macular organs but not cristae.
source: Using fluorescent in situ hybridization, we find that tectb is expressed in the macular organs but not cristae, and zpld1a is expressed in cristae but not maculae (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: zpld1a is expressed in cristae but not maculae.
source: Using fluorescent in situ hybridization, we find that tectb is expressed in the macular organs but not cristae, and zpld1a is expressed in cristae but not maculae (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Neither tectb nor zpld1a were detected in lateral line neuromasts.
source: Neither were detected in lateral line neuromasts (Figure 5C and D), showing they are inner ear-specific genes.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: tectb and zpld1a are inner ear-specific genes.
source: Neither were detected in lateral line neuromasts (Figure 5C and D), showing they are inner ear-specific genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of expression in lateral line neuromasts.

claim: Both tectb and zpld1a are expressed primarily in supporting cells.
source: Both tectb and zpld1a are expressed primarily in supporting cells, as they show little overlap in expression with the hair cell marker myo6b:GFP, similar to expression of the supporting cell marker lfng (Figure 5B–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Hair cells from the inner ear and lateral line form distinct clusters.
source: Using Scanorama for alignments (Hie et al., 2019), hair cells from the inner ear and lateral line form distinct clusters, with a number of differentially expressed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), including the known markers for lateral line (s100t) and inner ear (strc) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the Scanorama integration analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inner ear hair cells of the maculae and cristae are more similar to each other than to lateral line hair cells.
source: This analysis suggests that inner ear hair cells of the maculae and cristae are more similar to each other than to lateral line hair cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: Within the maculae and cristae, hair cells can be subdivided into two major groups (clusters 1 and 3 versus cluster 4).
source: Within the maculae and cristae, we find that hair cells can be subdivided into two major groups (clusters 1 and 3 versus cluster 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Hair cell clusters are distinguished by differential expression of a number of genes including two calcium binding protein genes, cabp1b and cabp2b.
source: These clusters are distinguished by differential expression of a number of genes including two calcium binding protein genes, cabp1b and cabp2b (Di Donato et al., 2013; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis, supported by a citation and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hair cell cluster 5 has a mixed identity with co-expression of a number of genes shared between the two major groups, including cabp1b and cabp2b.
source: Hair cell cluster 5 has a mixed identity with co-expression of a number of genes shared between these two groups, including cabp1b and cabp2b.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis.

claim: In the larval cristae, utricle, and saccule, cabp1b and cabp2b mark myo6b+ hair cells in largely non-overlapping zones.
source: In the larval cristae, utricle, and saccule, cabp1b and cabp2b mark myo6b+hair cells in largely non-overlapping zones (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: By adult stages, complementary domains of cabp1b+ and cabp2b+ hair cells become clearly apparent.
source: By adult stages, complementary domains of cabp1b+and cabp2b+hair cells become clearly apparent (Figure 6E–K).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6E–K.

claim: In the adult utricle, a central crescent of cabp2b+; myo6b+ hair cells is surrounded by a broad domain of cabp1b+; myo6b+ hair cells.
source: In the adult utricle, a central crescent of cabp2b+; myo6b+hair cells is surrounded by a broad domain of cabp1b+; myo6b+hair cells.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the saccule and lagena, central cabp2b+; myo6b+ hair cells are surrounded by peripheral cabp1b+; myo6b+ hair cells.
source: In the saccule and lagena, a late developing sensory organ, central cabp2b+; myo6b+hair cells are surrounded by peripheral cabp1b+; myo6b+hair cells.
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The calcium binding protein gene cabp5b is specific for hair cells in the cristae.
source: We also find several genes that are specific for hair cells in the cristae, utricle, or saccule (Figure 7A). These include the calcium binding protein gene cabp5b in the cristae, the transcription factor skor2 in the utricle, and the deafness gene loxhd1b in the saccule (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7.

claim: The transcription factor skor2 is specific for hair cells in the utricle.
source: We also find several genes that are specific for hair cells in the cristae, utricle, or saccule (Figure 7A). These include the calcium binding protein gene cabp5b in the cristae, the transcription factor skor2 in the utricle, and the deafness gene loxhd1b in the saccule (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7.

claim: The deafness gene loxhd1b is specific for hair cells in the saccule.
source: We also find several genes that are specific for hair cells in the cristae, utricle, or saccule (Figure 7A). These include the calcium binding protein gene cabp5b in the cristae, the transcription factor skor2 in the utricle, and the deafness gene loxhd1b in the saccule (Figure 7B–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis and in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7.

claim: The domain organization of hair cells in the adult macular organs resembles that of striolar and extrastriolar hair cells in the mammalian utricle.
source: The domain organization of hair cells in the adult macular organs resembles that of striolar and extrastriolar hair cells in the mammalian utricle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial patterns observed and comparison with mammalian anatomy.

claim: In the larval utricle, there is near complete overlap of pvalb9 with cabp2b.
source: In the larval utricle, we observe near complete overlap of pvalb9 with cabp2b (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 8B–D.

claim: In the adult utricle, there is substantial overlap of pvalb9 with cabp2b expression (except for a thin strip of pvalb9+; cabp2b- cells), and little overlap with cabp1b expression.
source: In the adult utricle, there is substantial overlap of pvalb9 with cabp2b expression (except for a thin strip of pvalb9+; cabp2b- cells), and little overlap with cabp1b expression (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: Anti-Spectrin staining of hair bundles reveals a line of polarity reversal within the cabp2b+ domain of the utricle.
source: In addition, anti-Spectrin staining of hair bundles reveals a line of polarity reversal within the cabp2b+domain of the utricle (Figure 8H, I), consistent with polarity reversal occurring within the striolar domains of mammalian macular organs (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 8H and I, supported by a citation.

claim: Polarity reversal occurs within the striolar domains of mammalian macular organs.
source: In addition, anti-Spectrin staining of hair bundles reveals a line of polarity reversal within the cabp2b+domain of the utricle (Figure 8H, I), consistent with polarity reversal occurring within the striolar domains of mammalian macular organs (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) and Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) populations differentially express genes related to stereocilia tip link and mechanotransduction channel components.
source: Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) and Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) populations also differentially express genes related to stereocilia tip link and mechanotransduction channel components (Figure 8—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 8) and various calcium and potassium channels (Figure 8—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) and Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) populations differentially express various calcium and potassium channels.
source: Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) and Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) populations also differentially express genes related to stereocilia tip link and mechanotransduction channel components (Figure 8—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 8) and various calcium and potassium channels (Figure 8—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: The utricle marker skor2 labels primarily extrastriolar hair cells within this end organ.
source: We also note that the utricle marker skor2 labels primarily extrastriolar hair cells within this end organ, with loxhd1b labeling striolar hair cells within the saccule.
evidence: This is a finding from the in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: loxhd1b labels striolar hair cells within the saccule.
source: We also note that the utricle marker skor2 labels primarily extrastriolar hair cells within this end organ, with loxhd1b labeling striolar hair cells within the saccule.
evidence: This is a finding from the in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) and Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells largely correspond to striolar and extrastriolar hair cells, respectively.
source: These findings suggest that zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) and Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells largely correspond to striolar and extrastriolar hair cells, respectively, with distinct mechanotransduction and synaptic properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression patterns and spatial organization observed.

claim: Mouse striolar Type I hair cells exclusively map to zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells.
source: Consistent with the spatial domains revealed by our in situ gene expression analysis, we find that mouse striolar Type I hair cells exclusively map to zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells, and mouse extrastriolar Type I and Type II hair cells predominantly to zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mouse extrastriolar Type I and Type II hair cells predominantly map to zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells.
source: Consistent with the spatial domains revealed by our in situ gene expression analysis, we find that mouse striolar Type I hair cells exclusively map to zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells, and mouse extrastriolar Type I and Type II hair cells predominantly to zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Zebrafish lateral line hair cells align exclusively to mouse extrastriolar and not striolar hair cells.
source: In contrast, zebrafish lateral line hair cells (Lush et al., 2019) align exclusively to mouse extrastriolar and not striolar hair cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1, supported by a citation.

claim: Zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells may have more of a Type I identity than Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) cells in general.
source: The small degree of mapping of mouse extrastriolar Type I hair cells to zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells suggests that zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells may have more of a Type I identity than Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) cells in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SAMap analysis results.

claim: Gene pairs driving the homology alignment include striolar markers Ocm, Loxhd1, and Atp2b2 for zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells.
source: Gene pairs driving the homology alignment include striolar markers Ocm, Loxhd1, and Atp2b2 for zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells, and mouse extrastriolar markers Tmc1, Atoh1, and Jag2 for zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis listed in Supplementary file 9.

claim: Gene pairs driving the homology alignment include mouse extrastriolar markers Tmc1, Atoh1, and Jag2 for zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells.
source: Gene pairs driving the homology alignment include striolar markers Ocm, Loxhd1, and Atp2b2 for zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) hair cells, and mouse extrastriolar markers Tmc1, Atoh1, and Jag2 for zebrafish Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) hair cells (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis listed in Supplementary file 9.

claim: Zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) macular hair cells are closely related to striolar cells of the mouse utricle.
source: Thus, zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) macular hair cells are closely related to striolar cells of the mouse utricle, with zebrafish lateral line and Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) macular hair cells more closely related to mouse extrastriolar hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAMap analysis.

claim: Zebrafish lateral line and Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) macular hair cells are more closely related to mouse extrastriolar hair cells.
source: Thus, zebrafish Cluster 4 (cabp2b+) macular hair cells are closely related to striolar cells of the mouse utricle, with zebrafish lateral line and Cluster 1/3 (cabp1b+) macular hair cells more closely related to mouse extrastriolar hair cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAMap analysis.

claim: A recent single-cell study revealed distinct central versus peripheral hair cell subpopulations in postnatal mouse cristae.
source: A recent single-cell study revealed distinct central versus peripheral hair cell subpopulations in postnatal mouse cristae, reminiscent of the striolar and extrastriolar populations in the maculae (Wilkerson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Zebrafish centrally located Cluster 8 crista hair cells predominantly map to mouse central crista hair cells.
source: Similar to what we observed for the utricle, zebrafish centrally located Cluster 8 crista hair cells predominantly map to mouse central crista hair cells, and zebrafish peripherally located Cluster 9 crista hair cells exclusively map to mouse peripheral crista hair cells (Figure 9B, see Supplementary file 10 for differentially expressed genes in Cluster 8 and Cluster 9 hair cells and Supplementary file 11 for gene pairs driving homology).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Zebrafish peripherally located Cluster 9 crista hair cells exclusively map to mouse peripheral crista hair cells.
source: Similar to what we observed for the utricle, zebrafish centrally located Cluster 8 crista hair cells predominantly map to mouse central crista hair cells, and zebrafish peripherally located Cluster 9 crista hair cells exclusively map to mouse peripheral crista hair cells (Figure 9B, see Supplementary file 10 for differentially expressed genes in Cluster 8 and Cluster 9 hair cells and Supplementary file 11 for gene pairs driving homology).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAMap analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Conserved types of spatially segregated hair cells exist in both the maculae and cristae of zebrafish and mouse.
source: Conserved types of spatially segregated HCs therefore exist in both the maculae and cristae of zebrafish and mouse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAMap analysis of both maculae and cristae.

claim: Understanding similarities and differences between the lateral line and inner ear has the potential to uncover mechanisms underlying the distinct regenerative capacity of inner ear hair cell subtypes.
source: As much of our knowledge about zebrafish hair cell regeneration comes from studies of the lateral line, understanding similarities and differences between the lateral line and inner ear has the potential to uncover mechanisms underlying the distinct regenerative capacity of inner ear hair cell subtypes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential implications of the findings.

claim: The study was not able to resolve distinct clusters of hair cells or supporting cells corresponding to the distinct types of maculae (utricle, saccule, and lagena).
source: However, consistent with other recent work (Jimenez et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2022), we were not able to resolve distinct clusters of hair cells or supporting cells corresponding to the distinct types of maculae: i.e. utricle, saccule, and lagena.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study, supported by citations to other recent work.

claim: The saccule is thought to act as the primary auditory organ of larval zebrafish.
source: The saccule is thought to act as the primary auditory organ of larval zebrafish, as the utricle is not necessary for sound detection above low frequencies (Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The utricle is not necessary for sound detection above low frequencies in larval zebrafish.
source: The saccule is thought to act as the primary auditory organ of larval zebrafish, as the utricle is not necessary for sound detection above low frequencies (Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In the zebrafish adult, excess sound exposure can damage the saccule.
source: In the zebrafish adult, excess sound exposure can damage the saccule, while damage to the utricle is unknown (Schuck and Smith, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The utricle is critical for larval vestibular function.
source: Conversely, the utricle is critical for larval vestibular function, while input from the saccule is unnecessary (Riley and Moorman, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Input from the saccule is unnecessary for larval vestibular function.
source: Conversely, the utricle is critical for larval vestibular function, while input from the saccule is unnecessary (Riley and Moorman, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There is contrasting evidence for overlap in function of both saccule and utricle for sound detection in larvae.
source: However, there is contrasting evidence for overlap in function of both saccule and utricle for sound detection in larvae (Favre-Bulle et al., 2020; Poulsen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian vestibular end organs are capable of responding to high-frequency sound stimuli.
source: It is interesting to note that mammalian vestibular end organs are also capable of responding to high-frequency sound stimuli (reviewed in Curthoys, 2017), suggesting that sound detection by hair cells may not be linked to a distinct end organ-specific molecular signature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Sound detection by hair cells may not be linked to a distinct end organ-specific molecular signature.
source: It is interesting to note that mammalian vestibular end organs are also capable of responding to high-frequency sound stimuli (reviewed in Curthoys, 2017), suggesting that sound detection by hair cells may not be linked to a distinct end organ-specific molecular signature.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation about mammalian vestibular organs.

claim: In the zebrafish utricle, vibration is preferentially transduced by striolar cells while static tilt is received by extrastriolar cells.
source: In the zebrafish utricle, vibration is preferentially transduced by striolar cells while static tilt is received by extrastriolar cells (Tanimoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: s100s is a highly specific marker for striolar hair cells.
source: Consistent with use of a s100s-hs:tdTomato transgene to mark striolar cells in this previous study, s100s is a highly specific marker for our striolar hair cell cluster (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Zebrafish striolar and extrastriolar hair cell subtypes express distinct combinations of ion channel genes and mechanotransduction components.
source: We also find zebrafish striolar and extrastriolar hair cell subtypes express distinct combinations of ion channel genes and mechanotransduction components, consistent with previous reports of distinct current profiles in central versus peripheral hair cells in the zebrafish utricle, saccule, and lagena (Haden et al., 2013; Olt et al., 2014), as well as spatial differences in ciliary bundle morphology and synaptic innervation in the larval zebrafish utricle (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous reports show distinct current profiles in central versus peripheral hair cells in the zebrafish utricle, saccule, and lagena.
source: We also find zebrafish striolar and extrastriolar hair cell subtypes express distinct combinations of ion channel genes and mechanotransduction components, consistent with previous reports of distinct current profiles in central versus peripheral hair cells in the zebrafish utricle, saccule, and lagena (Haden et al., 2013; Olt et al., 2014), as well as spatial differences in ciliary bundle morphology and synaptic innervation in the larval zebrafish utricle (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are spatial differences in ciliary bundle morphology and synaptic innervation in the larval zebrafish utricle.
source: We also find zebrafish striolar and extrastriolar hair cell subtypes express distinct combinations of ion channel genes and mechanotransduction components, consistent with previous reports of distinct current profiles in central versus peripheral hair cells in the zebrafish utricle, saccule, and lagena (Haden et al., 2013; Olt et al., 2014), as well as spatial differences in ciliary bundle morphology and synaptic innervation in the larval zebrafish utricle (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The distinct spatial distribution, channel expression, and hair bundle morphologies in zebrafish hair cells resemble the known spatial, electrophysiological, and hair bundle compositional differences seen in the striolar versus extrastriolar hair cells in the amniote vestibular end organs.
source: The distinct spatial distribution, channel expression, and hair bundle morphologies in these hair cells resembles the known spatial, electrophysiological, and hair bundle compositional differences seen in the striolar versus extrastriolar hair cells in the amniote vestibular end organs (Holt et al., 2007; Kharkovets et al., 2000; Lapeyre et al., 1992; Meredith and Rennie, 2016; Moravec and Peterson, 2004; Rüsch et al., 1998; Xue and Peterson, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Calcium binding proteins closely interact with synaptic calcium channels.
source: As these calcium binding proteins closely interact with synaptic calcium channels (Cui et al., 2007; Picher et al., 2017) with potential functionally different consequences (Yang et al., 2018), their differential expression may confer unique electrophysiological properties to each cell type.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Differential expression of calcium binding proteins may confer unique electrophysiological properties to each cell type.
source: As these calcium binding proteins closely interact with synaptic calcium channels (Cui et al., 2007; Picher et al., 2017) with potential functionally different consequences (Yang et al., 2018), their differential expression may confer unique electrophysiological properties to each cell type.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known interactions of calcium binding proteins with calcium channels.

claim: Mutations in human CABP2 associated with the autosomal recessive locus DFNB93 result in hearing loss.
source: Mutations in human CABP2 associated with the autosomal recessive locus DFNB93 result in hearing loss (Schrauwen et al., 2012; Picher et al., 2017), underlining its functional importance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cabp2, but not Cabp1, is expressed in all mouse postnatal utricular hair cells with differentially higher expression in the striola.
source: Even though we chose cabp1b and cabp2b as characteristic markers for zebrafish extrastriolar and striolar regions, it is worth noting that Cabp2, but not Cabp1, is expressed in all mouse postnatal utricular hair cells with differentially higher expression in the striola (Jan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Lateral line hair cells express higher levels of cabp2b than cabp1b.
source: Of note, lateral line hair cells express higher levels of cabp2b than cabp1b (Lush et al., 2019), despite our analysis suggesting that they are more closely related to extrastriolar hair cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The lack of molecular signatures corresponding to Type I hair cells is consistent with previous reports that calyx synapses are absent from macular organs in fishes.
source: The lack of molecular signatures corresponding to Type I hair cells is consistent with previous reports that one of their major features, calyx synapses, are absent from macular organs in fishes (Lysakowski and Goldberg, 2004, but see Lanford and Popper, 1996 for evidence of calyx synapses in goldfish cristae).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of Type I signatures and prior knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The diversification of inner ear hair cells into Type I and Type II cells may have largely emerged after the evolutionary split of ray-finned fishes from the lineage leading to mammals.
source: These findings suggest that the diversification of inner ear hair cells into Type I and Type II cells may have largely emerged after the evolutionary split of ray-finned fishes from the lineage leading to mammals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the absence of Type I/Type II distinction in zebrafish.

claim: The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Southern California (Protocol 20771) and University of Washington (Protocol 2997–01) approved all animal experiments.
source: The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of the University of Southern California (Protocol 20771) and University of Washington (Protocol 2997–01) approved all animal experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: Experiments were performed on zebrafish (Danio rerio) of AB or mixed AB/Tubingen background.
source: Experiments were performed on zebrafish (Danio rerio) of AB or mixed AB/Tubingen background.
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: For adult stages, mixed sexes of animals were used for constructing single-cell libraries, as well as RNAScope experiments.
source: For adult stages, mixed sexes of animals were used for constructing single-cell libraries, as well as RNAScope experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.
